title: My family sim killed a soldier’s wife while he waited overseas in 1947. Nobody wrote that. Here’s how the numbers got there.
author: MDawg74
selftext:
"Kinfolks" is a text sim of one Appalachian family over a hundred years and more. I built it with Claude. It’s one HTML file, about 18,000 lines, that runs in the browser with no server, and it never calls an AI while you play. Last night it handed me a story I didn’t write, so I went back through the code to see how it got there. That’s what this post is about.

**How it was put together**

Before most systems went in, we researched them. The game sits on about two dozen research files: dated timelines from 1860 to 2020, wages and money, feuds, law and liquor, granny medicine, foodways and the farm year, names and nicknames, clothes by decade, church and music, the railroads and the mines. A rule doesn’t go in unless there’s a source behind it. If it’s thin or dubious, it stays out.

Then we tested the odds. We ran 300 simulated family books and compared them with what really happened. One early build had 13% of the men sent to WWII dying. The real number, all causes, from the VA, is 2.5%. Another had a family go from 1860 to 1976 without anybody ever going to a war. Each row that was off got fixed against its source.

Players shaped it too. One said the book read like a machine wrote it, and she was right, so the game now has a writing standard: a county register kept by somebody on the family’s side, where an entry says what happened and stops. Another player noticed WWI came and went with nothing happening, so the home front went in: the registration days, the meatless Tuesdays, the Liberty Bonds.

**The war takes men one at a time**

Every year of a war, each man in the draft ages gets his own roll at the rate men his age actually went. From 1942 to 1945 that band is 18 to 37. A coal miner is deferred three times out of four, because the coal face needed him. A house is never stripped down to one pair of hands.

Luther Sturgill turned 18 in August 1944, and the draft took him on June 6, 1945. Going in that late, he had few points. Under the Army’s point system the men with the most service went home first, and late draftees stayed overseas on occupation duty. In July 1947 he’s still gone. His people hung a service flag with a blue star in the window and sent him a box with a cake and a pair of socks, in 1945 and again in 1946.

He wasn’t the only one away. Pa Coy went to the war in 1943. Garland went to Ohio for work that year, the way a lot of mountain people did. By 1947 every grown man in the house was gone.

**Feuds climb a ladder**

A grudge starts at 3 points and each rung adds 2. Left alone, a feud climbs one rung a year. Nothing happens before the fourth rung, and after that the chance of a killing rises 5% per rung. Most feuds wear out before they get there. Every year a family carries one, its standing at church and on the creek wears down, which is why settling is worth doing.

**Then there’s the player’s hand**

When a feud card comes up you can settle, take it to the law, let it lay, or Stand on it. The game never pretends the family chose. It writes that a hand from outside reached into the holler, and a bad choice gets the dark version more often than not: “The Devil had cursed Ma Arminta to have it out with the Damrons.” “Bad luck had been savin’ itself up.” Standing on it climbs a rung the same day and puts the card right back in front of you. The log shows I stood on it four times on July 2, 1947. That part is on me.

**Who it fell on**

When a feud turns deadly, the game picks from who’s home between 15 and 65. Men count six to one, and anybody 17 to 45 counts double, because that’s who was in it. Anybody away doesn’t count at all. The war and Ohio had taken every man of age, so the house was women. Loretta, 21, died in the trouble with the Damrons. Her mother, Ma Arminta, the one who wouldn’t let it lay, was found on the road.

Nobody wrote “the war left the women to face the feud.” The rule about who’s home did that, and that’s how it went in a lot of real houses during the war.

**One record, a lot of ways to read it**

Every event is written once, onto the people in it. The log shows it as it happens. Each person has a book with every line about them in order, and Luther’s runs from his wedding to the draft to the blue star to the boxes. The buryin’ ground has a stone for each of the dead, with their dates, how they died, who they married and who their mother was. That’s how I found out Arminta was Loretta’s mother. I didn’t know until I opened the stone.

The portrait button reads the same record. The year picks the kind of photograph, the face comes off the character card, and the clothes are said plainly. The game writes the prompt and I pasted it into ChatGPT. Luther sat for a studio picture in his good shirt. Loretta’s is a snapshot took on the place, in her apron.

**Where the AI fits**

Claude wrote the code with me. I set the rules, checked the history and kept testing it. The story at the end isn’t an AI writing fiction. It’s real dates, real rates and a handful of plain rules running into each other in one family, and then me pressing a button I shouldn’t have.

Full story with the game’s own pages: [https://mdawg74.itch.io/kinfolks/devlog/1751390/singin-luther-sturgill-went-to-war-the-feud-came-to-his-house](https://mdawg74.itch.io/kinfolks/devlog/1751390/singin-luther-sturgill-went-to-war-the-feud-came-to-his-house)

Free to play in the browser: [https://mdawg74.itch.io/kinfolks](https://mdawg74.itch.io/kinfolks)

For anyone building sims like this: how do you check your odds against real history? We ran batches of simulated families and compared. I’m curious what other people do.
